::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Rising air expands against lower pressure and does work, so it cools without losing any heat to its surroundings. Where that cooling crosses the dew point is the cloud base.
:::

## Adiabatic expansion

The atmosphere is not cooled by refrigerators; it is cooled by **expansion against decreasing ambient pressure**.

When a parcel of warm air rises, the surrounding atmospheric pressure drops exponentially with height ($P(z) = P_0 e^{-z/H}$). As the parcel expands, it performs mechanical work on the surrounding air ($W = P \Delta V$). Because air is a poor conductor of heat, this process is **adiabatic** ($dQ = 0$):

$$dU = - dW \implies m c_v dT = - P dV$$

```
Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR, Γ_d):
Γ_d = - dT/dz = g / c_p ≈ 9.8 °C / km  (~ 1 °C per 100 meters)

Saturated / Moist Adiabatic Lapse Rate (MALR, Γ_m):
Γ_m = - dT/dz ≈ 4 to 7 °C / km  (Lower due to latent heat release!)
```

## The lifting condensation level

The altitude at which a rising air parcel's temperature $T$ cools down to its **dew point** $T_d$ is the **Lifting Condensation Level (LCL)**—this marks the flat bottom (cloud base) of cumulus clouds:

$$z_{\text{LCL}} \approx \frac{T_0 - T_{d0}}{\Gamma_d - \Gamma_{\text{dew}}} \approx 125 \times (T_0 - T_{d0}) \text{ meters}$$

If surface temperature $T_0 = 25^\circ\text{C}$ and dew point $T_{d0} = 17^\circ\text{C}$:

$$z_{\text{LCL}} \approx 125 \times (25 - 17) = 1,000 \text{ meters above ground}$$

## Key takeaways

- A rising parcel cools because it expands and does work on the surrounding air, not because it loses heat; the process is adiabatic.
- Dry air cools at $\Gamma_d = g/c_p \approx 9.8^\circ\text{C km}^{-1}$; once condensation starts, latent heat release slows this to roughly $4$ to $7^\circ\text{C km}^{-1}$.
- The cloud base sits where temperature meets dew point, at $z_{\text{LCL}} \approx 125\,(T_0 - T_{d0})$ metres, so an $8^\circ\text{C}$ spread puts the base near $1\text{ km}$.
- Every parcel with the same surface temperature and humidity condenses at the same height, which is why cumulus bases are flat.
